content: 1. For individuals who are on insulin therapy or are at high risk of hypoglycemia, it is essential to review their history of hypoglycemic episodes during every clinical visit. This practice ensures timely interventions and necessary adjustments to their treatment plans, thereby reducing the likelihood of future hypoglycemic events. 2. Screening for impaired hypoglycemia awareness should be conducted in individuals at high risk. This screening identifies those who may not recognize hypoglycemia symptoms until their blood glucose levels drop to dangerously low levels, enabling proactive management and treatment. 3. Clinicians should carefully consider an individual’s risk of hypoglycemia when selecting diabetes medications and setting glycemic targets. Certain medications carry a higher risk of hypoglycemia, and establishing appropriate blood glucose goals can help mitigate these risks. 4. Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) is recommended for individuals at high risk of hypoglycemia. CGM provides real-time glucose data, allowing for timely adjustments in treatment or lifestyle to prevent hypoglycemic events. 5. In cases of hypoglycemia, immediate treatment with fast-acting glucose sources, such as glucose tablets or juice, is advised. If symptoms persist after 15 minutes, the glucose treatment should be repeated to restore safe blood sugar levels. 6. Glucagon should be prescribed to all individuals at high risk of severe hypoglycemia. Family members and caregivers must be trained on how to administer glucagon, as it is a critical intervention during emergencies when the individual is unable to self-treat. 7. Comprehensive education on hypoglycemia prevention and management should be provided to all individuals at risk. This includes training on recognizing early symptoms and the proper use of glucagon in cases of severe hypoglycemia. 8. If an individual experiences two or more episodes of level 2 or level 3 hypoglycemia (significantly low blood sugar), their treatment plan should be reassessed. This reassessment may involve adjusting or switching medications to better manage their condition. 9. Individuals with impaired awareness of hypoglycemia should be referred to healthcare professionals for behavioral interventions. These interventions aim to restore the ability to recognize early symptoms of hypoglycemia, thereby preventing severe episodes. 10. Regular assessment of cognitive function is recommended for individuals at risk of hypoglycemia. Cognitive impairment can hinder self-management and increase the risk of adverse outcomes during hypoglycemic episodes.
